howto.name: Choose v4 or v7-like
howto.text: Pick the variant. v4, the default, is a random UUID from the browser's crypto.randomUUID(). v7-like starts with the current time in milliseconds, so IDs made in a later millisecond sort after earlier ones.

howto.name: Set how many to make
howto.text: Type a count from 1 to 500; the page opens with 10 v4 UUIDs. A number above 500 is lowered to 500, 0 or a blank box becomes 1, and decimals are cut to whole numbers.

howto.name: Generate a fresh list
howto.text: A new list appears as soon as you change the count or variant, and Regenerate makes another with the same settings. The header above the list shows how many UUIDs it holds.

howto.name: Copy the whole list
howto.text: Copy puts every UUID on your clipboard, one lowercase UUID per line with no trailing line break, ready for SQL, a spreadsheet or a test fixture. There is no download button. If the browser blocks clipboard access, the tool asks you to select the list and copy it yourself.

faq.q: What is the difference between v4 and v7-like?
faq.a: Under RFC 9562, a v4 UUID is 122 random bits plus 6 fixed version and variant bits, so it reveals nothing about when it was made and has no meaningful order. A v7-like ID begins with a millisecond Unix timestamp, so sorting the IDs as text also sorts them by creation time. Time-ordered IDs are often chosen as database keys, at the cost of showing when each one was created.

faq.q: How exactly is a v7-like ID built?
faq.a: It is 32 lowercase hex digits in the 8-4-4-4-12 pattern. The first 12 digits (48 bits) hold the current Unix time in milliseconds. The 13th digit is always 7, the version. The first digit of the fourth group is 8, 9, a or b, which sets the two variant bits to 10. The remaining 18 digits, and the last two bits of that variant digit, come from crypto.getRandomValues.

faq.q: How do I read the time in a v7-like ID?
faq.a: Join the first two groups and read them as one hexadecimal number of milliseconds since 1 January 1970 UTC. In 01a0d349-6e00-73f2-ba9c-1122d5667788, 01a0d3496e00 is 1790251200000, which is 2026-09-24 12:00:00.000 UTC. That is the exact ID the tool builds at that moment from the random bytes 3f 2a 9c 11 22 d5 66 77 88 99.

faq.q: Is the v7-like format RFC 9562 compliant?
faq.a: Its layout matches RFC 9562 version 7: a 48-bit millisecond timestamp, version 7, variant 10 and random bits, so UUID parsers read it as version 7. It is labelled v7-like because it is not a complete implementation. There is no counter, so IDs created in the same millisecond, which is common within one list, are in random order relative to each other. And the two bits after the variant repeat two bits found later in the same ID, leaving 72 independent random bits instead of the RFC's 74.

Negligible for normal use. With 122 random bits, the birthday bound says about 2.7 × 10^18 v4 UUIDs must exist before the chance of any duplicate reaches 50%. A v7-like ID can only collide with another from the same millisecond, and each carries 72 independent random bits.
Yes. v4 comes from the browser's crypto.randomUUID() and the random part of v7-like IDs from crypto.getRandomValues, both cryptographically secure parts of the Web Crypto API.

faq.q: Why do my v7-like IDs start with the same digits?
faq.a: The first 12 hex digits are the timestamp, so IDs made in the same millisecond share all of them, and IDs made moments apart share the leading ones. Only the random digits after the second hyphen tell those IDs apart.

faq.q: Is anything sent to a server?
faq.a: No. Both variants are generated by JavaScript in your browser and the tool makes no network request. The list exists only on this page until you copy it; regenerating or reloading replaces it.
